--- format: html echo: true lang: en --- ## Lab 12 -- Estimating abundance with closed-population capture-mark-recapture data
Due by 5:00pm on Friday The purpose of this lab is to learn how to estimate abundance using mark-recapture data from surveys of closed populations. A closed population does not experience recruitment, mortality, immigration or emigration. The closure assumption is usually only valid over very short time periods. We will learn how to work with data from open populations later. Work through the problems below, put your code and your answers in a Word file, and then upload it to ELC. Name the file something like "Chandler-lab.docx". Feel free to use R Markdown if you wish. ### Assignment #### Exercise I: Lincoln-Peterson estimation 1. Suppose you capture, mark, and release 100 largemouth bass (*Micropterus salmoides*) at Lake Herrick. The next day, you return and capture 50 individuals, 25 of which were marked on the first occasion. What is the Lincoln-Peterson estimate of abundance ($N$)? Do the calculations in R and show your work. #### Exercise II: Closed-population models in R * Use the R package "Rcapture" to fit the four mark-recapture models described in Table~\ref{tab:Otis} to the stinkpot (*Sternotherus odoratus*) data found in the file `CH-SO-Andy07.inp`. These data were collected using baited "hoop traps" at Andy's Pond in 2007. Software instructions are in the next section. * Summarize your results by creating a table in which each row is a model, and include the following columns: model description, the estimates of $N$ (abundance), the standard errors of $N$ (SE), and the AICc values. * Use model $M_t$ to make a graph of capture probability ($p_t$) at each time point. You can do this in either Excel or R. * The model with the lowest AICc is considered the best in the set of models. Which model has the lowest AICc? Do your results suggest that there was a behavioral (i.e., a trap-happy or trap-shy) response? Explain. * Why do you think model $M_0$ is the worst model in the set? Look at the capture histories when answering this question. Model | Description ----- | ---------------------- $M_0$ | The most basic model in which $p$ and $c$ are constant $M_t$ | $p$ differs among sampling occasions and $p_t=c_t$. $M_b$ | Behavioral response model in which $p$ and $c$ differ. Can describe trap happiness or trap shiness. $M_{tb}$ | A combination of models $M_t$ and $M_b$. {\bf Parameter definitions} * $p$ -- capture probability. The probability of capturing an individual on a single occasion * $p_t$ -- capture probability on occasion $t$ * $c$ -- recapture probability. The probability of capturing an individual that has been captured previously. * $n$ -- the number of individuals captured % * $f_0$ -- the number of individual not captured * $N$ -- abundance. The number of individuals in the population. %$N=n+f_0$. ![](figs/Stinkpot.jpg) ### Example analysis in R Open R and install the "Rcapture" package using the following command: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("Rcapture") ``` ::: Now load the package like so: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(Rcapture) ``` ::: The example bear data are formatted for program MARK, but we can import them using `read.table`. The only trick is to tell R that the capture histories should be treated as a character string, rather than as a numeric variable. The `colClasses` arguments let's us do that. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} capture.histories <- read.table("CH-example.inp", sep=" ", colClasses=c("character", "character"), col.names=c("ch", "freq")) ``` ::: It's a small dataset, so we can display it in full: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} capture.histories ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ch freq 1 101001 1; 2 100001 1; 3 100001 1; 4 010000 1; 5 101000 1; 6 010001 1; 7 001000 1; 8 001011 1; 9 000100 1; 10 001001 1; 11 001000 1; 12 000010 1; 13 000010 1; 14 000101 1; ``` ::: ::: We need to convert the capture histories from a character vector to a matrix. The following code does the trick. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ch.mat <- t(sapply(capture.histories$ch, function(x) as.integer(strsplit(x, "")[[1]]))) dimnames(ch.mat) <- list(paste0("Bear", 1:nrow(capture.histories)), paste0("Time", 1:6)) ``` ::: Now the capture histories look like this: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ch.mat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time1 Time2 Time3 Time4 Time5 Time6 Bear1 1 0 1 0 0 1 Bear2 1 0 0 0 0 1 Bear3 1 0 0 0 0 1 Bear4 0 1 0 0 0 0 Bear5 1 0 1 0 0 0 Bear6 0 1 0 0 0 1 Bear7 0 0 1 0 0 0 Bear8 0 0 1 0 1 1 Bear9 0 0 0 1 0 0 Bear10 0 0 1 0 0 1 Bear11 0 0 1 0 0 0 Bear12 0 0 0 0 1 0 Bear13 0 0 0 0 1 0 Bear14 0 0 0 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: We will use the `closedp` function to fit the closed population models. This returns abundance estimates, standard errors (stderr), and AIC values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mods <- closedp(ch.mat) mods ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of captured units: 14 Abundance estimations and model fits: abundance stderr deviance df AIC BIC infoFit M0 18.0 3.1 29.771 61 57.612 58.890 OK Mt 17.4 2.8 22.692 56 60.533 65.007 OK Mh Chao (LB) 18.0 3.1 29.771 61 57.612 58.890 OK Mh Poisson2 15.6 2.3 28.704 60 58.545 60.462 OK Mh Darroch 15.0 2.0 28.836 60 58.677 60.594 OK Mh Gamma3.5 14.7 1.6 28.896 60 58.737 60.654 OK Mth Chao (LB) 17.4 2.8 22.692 56 60.533 65.007 OK Mth Poisson2 15.5 2.2 21.839 55 61.681 66.793 OK Mth Darroch 15.0 2.0 21.962 55 61.803 66.915 OK Mth Gamma3.5 14.7 1.7 22.015 55 61.856 66.969 OK Mb 17.2 4.4 29.730 60 59.572 61.489 OK Mbh 16.7 6.6 29.698 59 61.539 64.095 OK ``` ::: ::: You can extract parameter estimates for a model like this: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mods$parameters$M0, digits=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` N p estimate: 17.962 0.223 ``` ::: ::: For model $M_0$, capture probability is the same for all individuals during all time periods. This won't be the case for the other models. Here are the estimates for model $M_t$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mods$parameters$Mt, digits=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` N p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6 estimate: 17.404 0.23 0.115 0.345 0.115 0.172 0.402 ``` ::: ::: And model $M_b$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mods$parameters$Mb, digits=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` N p c estimate: 17.151 0.246 0.217 ``` ::: ::: We can get more information about a specific model using the function `closedpCI.t`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Mt <- closedpCI.t(ch.mat, m="Mt") Mt ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of captured units: 14 Poisson estimation and model fit: abundance stderr deviance df AIC BIC infoFit Mt 17.4 2.8 22.692 56 60.533 65.007 OK Multinomial estimation, 95% profile likelihood confidence interval: abundance infCL supCL infoCI Mt 16.4 14 25.2 warning #5 ``` ::: :::
